newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BANK INFLATION TALK WARNING TO UNIONS-ETLA.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BANK INFLATION TALK WARNING TO UNIONS-ETLA.

text.p: Finnish core inflation will run at over two percent next year as projected by the Bank of Finland on Monday only if import prices or wages rise more than expected, a leading economic think-tank said on Thursday.

The Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (ETLA) said in its monthly financial markets review that the central bank's inflation view was mainly a warning against excessive nominal pay rises ahead of the autumn round of collective bargaining.
"The Bank of Finland has raised eyebrows this week by emphasising the dangers of inflation," ETLA said.
"The two percent underlying inflation scenario of the Bank of Finland will occur only if import prices begin to rise steeply or if wages increase more than previously estimated," it said.
"For this reason the statement is generally regarded as a warning shot across the bows of the labour unions and employers confederation before pay talks get under way this autumn," it added.
ETLA said the Finnish central bank's inflation views "stand in contradiction with the mood elsewhere in Europe."
"The need to tighten monetary policy appears to be abating elsewhere in Europe as inflation has slowed down in the beginning of this year and concerns about unemployment have increased," it said.
In the run-up to EMU, a unilateral monetary policy tightening in Finland was not very likely, ETLA said.
"The coordination of monetary policy will shift to the European Central Bank soon after the EMU countries are selected," it said.
It was difficult to imagine the Bank of Finland bucking the trend in Europe by tightening the monetary policy screws, especially if Finland was deemed eligible for EMU in the first round, it said.

"The unilateral tightening of monetary policy in Finland prior to formation of EMU does not seem to be very likely, because after joining EMU Finland would probably be obliged to do an about-face and ease its monetary policy once again," ETLA said.
